translation_text:
### Introduction

The wild Indians of the plains of the Caquetá and the Putumayo, toward the south of the Republic, drink — to bring on a particular state of intoxication — the decoction and maceration of a plant called Yagé, to which they attribute marvelous properties confirmed by the tradition of various tribes.

Accounts from serious and educated persons all agree that this plant produces above all dreams and visual hallucinations, in which the individual under the effect of any one of its preparations sees things that do not belong to the primitive civilization surrounding him, but rather to a more complex one.

Yagé is a vine, a climbing plant, whose botanical classification has not yet been made. That field of experiment is left to the botanist. It appears to be an aristolochia, judging by certain details of its anatomical and histological structure: in cross-section its woody bundles are arranged in a ring.

The first person among us to undertake its study was Dr. Rafael Zerda Bayón, of cherished memory, a true man of science, who spent most of his life observing nature with the conviction that he would one day wrest some of its hidden secrets from it.

He made a celebrated scientific expedition to the Caquetá and the Putumayo with the purpose, among many others, of studying more closely and in detail the active principle of this plant. It was the object of profound and painstaking work, through which he came to suppose, after multiple experiments that did not succeed in isolating it, that this plant must contain as its active principle an alkaloid, which he christened telepatina [telepathine] for the very particular and curious effects produced by the ingestion of its preparations.

Out of respect for the memory of that illustrious scholar, the alkaloid we have isolated — and whose existence he supposed — should keep the name telepatina.

_[The author here thanks his thesis director, Dr. Eduardo Lleras Codazzi. Chapters I through III are omitted here as not bearing directly on the drug itself: a general account of alkaloids and their physiological action (Chapter I), a detailed account of the chemical procedure for extracting the yagé alkaloid (Chapter II), and toxicity experiments performed on frogs, rats, rabbits, and dogs (Chapter III). Chapter III concludes by noting that in animals the substance produces tremor, loss of balance, and motor incoordination, and, at the highest doses, a sleep broken by "sudden starts," but no deaths at the doses tested.]_

### Chapter IV. Action of the Yagé Alkaloid on the Human Organism

**First observation.** Mr. N. N., aged 24, weighing 64 kilos. He took 60 drops of an aqueous solution of Yagé by mouth and had the following symptoms: twenty minutes after ingesting the preparation he began to feel an extraordinary sense of well-being, mixed with great optimism about the events of his present life and his future, and an increase in memory and intellectual faculties. When walking it seemed to him as though he were walking on air and that his limbs scarcely touched the ground. After thirty minutes he lay down, because he began to have certain subjective sensations: an excessive swelling of the head and an unpleasant dizzy sensation; a heavy sleep then took hold of him, and he had the following hallucination, which he describes thus:

"I began to dream that I had turned into a gigantic man, whose height far surpassed that of the tallest buildings, and at my feet I beheld a multitude of pygmies moving in different directions, who raised their tiny faces to look at me in astonishment and then burst into loud laughter. Then came a gap, of who knows how much time, and I saw on the desk of my room two very small figures, no taller than ten centimeters each, a man and a woman, dressed thus: the woman in a yellow jacket, fitted at the waist, and a skirt of the same color with black ruffles, green stockings, and green slippers; the man in a fitted frock coat and knee-breeches, both green, with red stockings and black shoes. They danced merrily and looked at me smiling, with the utmost coquetry."

The next day I woke up with a slight headache, which lasted until midday.

**Second observation.** The author of this study, one night on going to bed, took a dose of about 10 grams of an aqueous solution, and after 15 minutes began to see blue spots on everything around him, accompanied by hemianopia and numbness in the lower limbs, fatigue and anxiety with precordial oppression that hindered his breathing, dryness in the larynx, heat in the epigastrium and intestinal colic, a slowing of the pulse, ringing in the ears, and a strange sensation in the scalp, as if it were tightly stretched and pressed against the cranial vault like a cap. A slight chill ran from the nape of the neck to the buttocks like a thread of water. Sensibility remained intact. These symptoms made him understand that he had entered the period of intoxication. On rising from bed, a dizzy sensation prevented him from walking quickly. Rapid measures taken to evacuate the toxin did not permit any accentuation or increase of these unpleasant phenomena. Even so, a heavy, gravitating headache eventually appeared, localized especially in the right frontal region, and it persisted — though not with the same intensity — until the afternoon of the following day.

**Third observation.** Mr. N. N., a medical student, was very keen to try the effects of the alkaloid, and for that purpose was given a small quantity of a slightly acidic solution, with the warning not to exceed, in 24 hours, a dose of more than 40 or 50 drops. Here is his account:

"I confess that on the first night chosen for the experiment, as I was retiring, I was seized by the fear that the preparation might poison me. After much hesitation, and with my nerves excessively on edge, I finally resolved, hoping for a bizarre, hallucinatory dream, to take only 25 drops.

"I lay down regretting having drunk the preparation, but what was my surprise when, about a quarter of an hour after ingesting it, I felt a great calm, a state of true euphoria that contrasted with my earlier panic. And so great was my serenity that I almost instinctively poured another 25 drops into a little water. I took my pulse. My heart rate, which only a moment before had been 98, had dropped to 76.

"But despite my tranquility, no hallucinations or illusions came, either before or during normal sleep. At three in the morning a hospital orderly came to wake me to attend to a seriously wounded man. I got up without the slightest discomfort or sluggishness, laughing to myself at this so-called Yagé; nevertheless, the following night, on going to bed, I resolved to take the substance again.

"This time I swallowed 50 drops in a single draught. Sleep came as usual, without the least hallucination. I only experienced again the same state of calm and indifference as the day before.

"I must confess that very, very rarely do I manage to dream anything at all. As a rule I sleep through the night without the slightest image or the faintest illusion appearing in that sleep. Perhaps for that very reason, I was able to notice, on three consecutive nights of taking yagé, that during sleep I returned to a clear and precise representation of whatever more important events I had seen or experienced while awake. The most significant things in my daily life would resurface at night, during sleep, with the same precision with which one watches, on a cinema screen, the sight of a place or a building that is familiar to us.

"On the first night, when the orderly came to wake me to attend to the wounded man, after giving him the necessary help I returned to my room and fell asleep again. Well then — although at the time I paid it no mind — I later remembered that I had dreamed of that wounded man exactly as I had seen him while treating him: with his penetrating chest wound, his labored breathing, and his anguished face.

"The next day I was at a social gathering, and that night, no doubt under the influence of the yagé, I again saw that gathering in detail, with the same people and with astonishingly sharp detail.

"On the third day I passed the time reading an interesting chapter of *The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse*. In that chapter Blasco Ibáñez masterfully recounts an attack on a castle in France. Well then, while asleep, the scene painted by Blasco Ibáñez reappeared with total clarity; I saw myself again holding the novel, reading that chapter.

"In summary: with the 150 drops of the Yagé preparation that I ingested, I was able to notice, over three nights, that I went back to dreaming of the most important things I had seen, felt, or read during the course of the day. It should also be noted that the plant exerts a sedative effect on the nervous system, since otherwise the general sense of well-being it produces cannot be explained. My morning urine had a slight olive-green color and had increased in quantity."

**Fourth observation.** Mr. N. N., weighing 70 kilos, a timber merchant. On the first night he took 25 drops of an aqueous solution of yagé and, after half an hour, began to feel a sensation of well-being and calm. He fell asleep very quickly and dreamed, with great clarity, of taking a trip to a beautiful town, where everything he saw surprised him with its novelty. The next day he woke up with no disturbance whatsoever.

**Fifth observation.** The same person, some nights later, took 40 drops of the same solution, experiencing, as before, well-being and calm, fullness of life and joy. Half an hour later he fell asleep and dreamed that he was in a beautiful town he had never known, with magnificent buildings and great crowds of people moving about, which in the dream he imagined to be in Mexico; but all with a perfect clarity, as though he were seeing it while awake. He says he had moments of something like half-wakefulness, in which he realized he had taken the drops of the yagé preparation and was troubled by the fear of poisoning himself — moments that passed quickly, giving way again to the dream of the same town with its sumptuous buildings. The next day he woke at his usual hour with a slight heaviness in his head.

**Sixth observation.** Mr. N. N., aged 42, weighing 66 kilos. One night, on going to bed, he took 50 drops of an aqueous solution of the alkaloid. Here is his description:

"Twenty minutes after taking the drops of the preparation with a little water, I began to feel a sensation so pleasant, so delightful, with such great lightness in all my movements, that it seemed as if I had suddenly grown young again.

"I took advantage of this state of euphoria to read a book I had at hand, and I noticed that I absorbed the passages passing before my eyes with great ease; but little by little a peaceful sleepiness began to overtake me at this task, and I decided to go to bed. Within five minutes at most I fell asleep, and I saw — something that has astonished me enormously — with startling clarity, a scene from my childhood that I had never dreamed of before and had always tried to forget in the course of my life since those events. Two people who had since died took part in it, whom I saw perfectly, with their most striking features and their complete, vivid countenance, with their characteristic gestures, as if I had seen them alive again at my side.

"After this scene had played out, I saw a crowd of very handsome men and beautiful women, dressed in bright colors, who, holding hands, whirled merrily around a gigantic wheel literally covered with yellow flowers as large as an open umbrella.

"I confess that I almost never dream, not even of the things that have most preoccupied me during the day, in the midst of life's cares, nor even when I fall asleep brooding over them, because the last thought always fades away with sleep without continuing into it."

**Seventh observation.** Mr. N. N., aged 23, weighing 52 kilos, of a very nervous temperament. One night he ingested 40 drops of an aqueous solution. Here is his account:

"I did not dare to take all at once the 40 or 50 drops I was told I could safely take, for fear of something strange happening to me — poisoning, for example. I decided to take it drop by drop, testing as I went, intending to stop as soon as I noticed any alarming symptom, but happily I found that as I increased the dose I became calmer and more serene. A short time later a somewhat heavy drowsiness came over me, along with a sensation of dizziness and malaise. I lay down, and with rest in bed these unpleasant symptoms diminished until I fell fully asleep and saw the following in a dream: I was walking through a field when suddenly a man of medium height appeared before me, with an enormous head and a highly ridiculous countenance: a parchment-like face covered in wrinkles, malevolent eyes that rolled continuously in their sockets in every direction, a sardonic smile. This disagreeable figure took to pursuing me wherever I went; I fled from him and hid wherever I could, but always, to my misfortune, ran into his repulsive figure again; disgusted and frightened, I would again try to shake him off, always with the same result.

"The next day I woke at my usual hour with a slight headache, still under the impression of the unpleasant dream that the Yagé preparation had given me."

_[A theoretical section follows in the original, "Considerations on the action of yagé in man," offering a general discussion of the physiology of sleep and a comparison between hashish and yagé; it is omitted here as it adds no new observations on the drug itself.]_

### General Conclusions on the Action of the Yagé Alkaloid

Absorption and elimination. — Absorption through the skin is nil. Absorption by the digestive route is rapid: general effects are already observed within 15 to 20 minutes. Absorption by the subcutaneous route generally takes between 10 and 15 minutes. Elimination occurs through the urine, to which it imparts a greenish-yellow coloration.

Toxicity. — Three centigrams of the alkaloid sulfate in aqueous solution produce loss of balance in the frog. A larger dose, seven centigrams, brings death within two hours, with stupor. Rats and rabbits given ten centigrams of the alkaloid sulfate in aqueous solution show symptoms of loss of balance, with tremor and motor incoordination. In man, ingestion of small doses produces dreams. High doses produce intoxication.

Digestive system. — Preparations of Yagé have a slightly bitter, pungent taste that provokes a reflex secretion of saliva. High doses cause heat in the epigastrium and mild intestinal colic.

Respiratory system. — In the frog, rat, and rabbit there is an increase in the rate of breathing. In man there is a slowing. High doses cause dryness of the larynx in the latter.

Small doses cause a decrease in pulse rate. In some cases blood pressure appears to increase.

Nervous system. — In small doses it produces an agreeable sensation of well-being and serenity, and pleasant dreams. In high doses there are hallucinations, headache, ringing in the ears, vertigo, precordial oppression and anxiety, and subjective sensations such as numbness of the lower limbs, visual disturbances — hemianopia and the perception of blue spots — and a sensation of cold across the back.

### Chapter 14. On the herb they call Ololiuhqui, which means 'plant of round leaves.'

Ololiuhqui, which others call cohuaxihuitl, meaning 'serpent herb,' is a twisting herb bearing thin, green, heart-shaped leaves; its stems are round, slender, and thin; its flowers are white, elongated, almost round, much like coriander, whence it took its name; its roots are thin as threads. This plant is hot in the fourth degree; it cures the French disease [syphilis]; it eases pains born of cold; it relieves flatulence and swelling. The powdered root, mixed with turpentine, expels cold, and is a great remedy for broken and dislocated bones, and for women's strained hips; the seed is also used in medicine, for, ground and drunk, or applied to the head, it cures ailments of the eyes; and drunk it also provokes lust; it is _[uncertain: "of such-and-such flavor"]_ and of an acidic and very hot temperament. Formerly the priests of the idols, who wished to commune with the devil and receive answers to their doubts, ate of this plant to go mad, and to see the thousand phantasms that appeared before them; and _[uncertain clause]_, this plant is nothing other than the maniacal _[uncertain: "Solanum"]_ of _[uncertain: "Dioscorides"]_. It will be no great error to omit saying here where it grows, since it would matter very little whether this herb were written of here at all, even if the Spaniards knew it.

translation_text:
### Le Gabon — Second Part (translated extract)

_[The chapter opens with a long account of Gabonese religion, fetish-huts, féticheurs and féticheuses, and a poison ordeal (icaja/m'boundou, a Strychnos), none of which concerns iboga; that material is omitted here. The extract below picks up where Griffon du Bellay surveys the country's food plants, oils and condiments, in the course of which he records the earliest published description of iboga as a stimulant.]_

If the social and intellectual life of black peoples always presents some interesting side, it is rare for their material life to be the same. I have shown how the Gabonese dress and house themselves; contact with Europeans has given them a taste for a certain relative comfort, but it has changed almost nothing in their mode of subsistence. In the midst of a vigorous and powerful nature, they have managed to create only resources insufficient for themselves and utterly nil for outsiders. Near their villages one sees hardly more than a few fine clumps of banana and manioc; within their compounds a few sacred trees, close by the fetish-hut, and a few ilangas, a liliaceous plant credited with the privilege of warding off lightning. The mango tree, introduced by Europeans, is beginning to appear there; the breadfruit tree has met less success, despite the generous efforts of the French Mission. On their holdings they cultivate, on a larger scale, the banana, manioc, yam, some groundnuts, maize and sugar-cane in small quantity, and finally a few aromatics.

These plots change place frequently, at the expense of the neighbouring forests. Such clearing is no mean labour. Whole villages migrate at once for this great undertaking and go to camp in the woods. Shelters are put up, roofed with the leaves of a very common balisier (a Canna-like plant), the ogongou. Some of the women busy themselves with cooking, while the others, carrying their children on their backs, go to help the men fell the trees they have cut down. In the evening the dances get under way to the sound of the tam-tam, for that is the conclusion of everything, of work as of pleasure. The fires blaze through the foliage and throw coppery gleams on these fearless dancers, their skin glistening with sweat, their gestures lascivious. Night and day it is a life, an animation unknown in the village. Everyone has driven off native laziness and works with ardour. But as soon as the clearing is opened and the heavy work finished, their natural bent returns at a gallop and the men go home to rest from their fatigues, leaving to the women alone the task of sowing the ground they have cleared by common effort.

It is, in sum, for the banana and the manioc that this activity develops. Both seem indigenous, though I have never met the banana tree except in places once under cultivation. This tree is, for the country, an immense resource. I was told of nineteen supposedly different species, and I myself had occasion to send several varieties to the Jardin d'Acclimatation at Algiers. Some bear enormous fruit, but none has the fine, delicate taste of the little banana so well known in our colonies under the name fig-banana or Freycinet fig. — Manioc has, over the American kind, the inestimable advantage of not being toxic. It undergoes a quite special preparation: it is reduced to a paste called gouma, after a preliminary maceration that gives it a certain degree of fermentation, and a sour, nauseous taste much appreciated by the natives. This, with dried fish and banana cooked before ripeness, is the basis of their diet.

Condiments are not lacking to this elementary cookery. There is perhaps no country richer in unexploited oil-bearing produce. From the crushed kernel of the Oba, a fine native mango-tree, is made dika, whose taste and colour recall chocolate — a remarkable product first made known by M. Aubry le Comte, today curator of the colonial exhibition. Two trees of the soapwort family [Sapotaceae], the djavé and the noungou, yield, the first a half-solid oil, the other a very firm fat of perfect whiteness. A very tall tree, the m'pôga, produces an excellent oil, though difficult to extract on account of the extreme hardness of the fruit that contains it. A leguminous tree, the owala, gives an enormous pod whose seeds are oily and edible. If to this quite incomplete list one adds the oil-palm, which is not very common, and the groundnut, which the natives care little for because it requires a certain amount of labour, one sees how rich this country is in vegetable fats, and what resources the inhabitants might find there if they were willing to take the trouble — not of cultivating, which is almost superfluous — but merely of multiplying and grouping the useful species.

Let us not close this review without speaking of the high-flavoured condiments the Gabon produces, though they are little used. First comes maketa, a golden ginger of good quality; then yangué-bère, énoné, and several other plants of the cardamom kind, whose hot, aromatic seeds are known in commerce under the names malaguetta, Guinea pepper, grains of paradise, etc., and were once much employed among us in pharmaceutical and culinary preparations. A tree of the custard-apple family, the ogana, produces pods of a somewhat coarse aroma. Nutmeg does not exist, I believe, in the country; yet two nutmeg-trees are found there, the combo and the niohué, whose nut is without scent but very oily. The vanilla vine is common, but not the vanilla. I have indeed very often come across this orchid without ever seeing its fruit. The women, who use its leaf in toilet preparations, do not know its pod or its scent. It is therefore likely that the natural fertilisation and fruiting of this plant are here even rarer than in the American species.

Sensual like Orientals, the Gabonese claims, like them, to possess remedies against physical failings. The most renowned aphrodisiac is the root of the ibôga (taberna-ventricosa, of the apocynaceous family). It is at the very least a general stimulant that might replace coffee; the natives use it on long canoe expeditions, to fight off sleep and revive their vigour. The fruits of several sterculias enjoy similar properties. The most esteemed is the red orendé. Another, the ombéné (Sterculia acuminata of Palisot de Beauvois), is well known under the name kola nut, or gourou. Its harsh, sweet taste strongly impregnates the papillae of the tongue and renders them momentarily insensible to disagreeable flavours. Brackish water then seems fresh and sweet — a precious property that makes this fruit sought after in the Sudan, where it is the object of an important trade. There is not a single traveller in that country, since René Caillé, who has not praised its virtues.

### On an intoxicating substance, banisterine, extracted from Banisteria Caapi

Note by Louis Lewin.

A South American plant, little known and not yet studied from a chemical and toxicological point of view, adds an interesting new member to the list of narcotic and stimulant principles. It is the liana *Banisteria Caapi*, of the family Malpighiaceae — a family in which no species of pronounced, even narcotic, toxicity had previously been recognized.

It grows wild or cultivated from the Orinoco to the Rio Negro and the Cordilleras, across a vast territory that takes in parts of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, southern Venezuela, western British Guiana, Brazil, and so on. In these countries, very diverse tribes use *Banisteria Caapi* as an intoxicant alongside tobacco, alcoholic drinks, and on occasion coca. By boiling and filtering the shredded, pulverized wood of the liana for seven or eight hours, they brew a potion drunk not only at communal festivals but also in private households. As much as a liter is sometimes consumed. It is said that this drink causes a trance state in which the drinker experiences agreeable and novel sensations. Ordinarily only men drink it; some tribes forbid it to women altogether. Two minutes after ingestion the Indian is seen to turn pale, tremble in every limb, sweat heavily, and fall into a violent fury. This excitation, lasting about ten minutes and accompanied by shouting, dancing, and perhaps cramps, is followed by exhaustion and a dreaming narcosis. At first one feels alternating sensations of heat and cold, with hallucinations and multiform visions and phantoms.

The active principle of *Banisteria Caapi*, banisterine, can be obtained in crystallized form, as prisms.

Its composition is as follows: C₁₃H₁₂ON₂. The melting point of the free base is 256°–257°; the hydrochloride melts at 264° while decomposing. According to Merck, this alkaloid is identical to harmine, extracted from *Peganum Harmala*. Pure sulfuric acid dissolves banisterine hydrochloride, producing a green fluorescence that soon disappears. After a few hours the colorless solution turns slightly violet.

The experiments I carried out on cold- and warm-blooded animals — including monkeys — showed without exception strong motor excitation accompanied by increased reflexes. Above all one notes tremors, which appear as early as 3–10 minutes and persist for up to two hours. Dogs fell into such a state of exasperation that they seemed rabid, and would have been killed had the cause of their condition not been known. To my knowledge, harmine does not produce comparable effects.

The men on whom I performed the experiment felt, after an injection of 0.02–0.07 g, a sensation of warmth and heaviness in the head and general lassitude. A woman suffering from hemiplegia had a spontaneous sensation of lightness; after the second injection she believed she could walk better and asked for a third. Professor Wilmans and Mr. Beringer carried out more extensive experiments. They found that banisterine slows the pulse, something I had already observed in animals and which may be of interest for the therapy of heart disease. But above all, persons suffering from an inflammation of the brain (*encephalitis lethargica*), the so-called cerebral influenza, felt better and lighter when treated with banisterine. The rigidity of the muscles, the most conspicuous symptom of this disease, diminished. Gait became freer and speech more distinct. At 0.04 g the rigidity nearly disappeared entirely. The remedies used up to now fall far short of banisterine.

It is not yet possible to specify the therapeutic applications of banisterine. It is likely that its use will meet with some success in certain paralyses.

_[Author's footnote in the original:]_ Mr. R. Hamet has studied some of the properties of *Banisteria Caapi* (*Comptes rendus*, 184, 1927, p. 1266).

translation_text:
IMPERIAL PATENT OFFICE.

PATENT SPECIFICATION No. 274350 — CLASS 12g, GROUP 32/70.

Firm E. Merck, of Darmstadt.

Process for the preparation of alkyloxyaryl-, dialkyloxyaryl- and alkylenedioxyarylaminopropanes, and their N-monoalkylated derivatives.

Patented in the German Reich from 24 December 1912.

The literature has repeatedly described the addition of two atoms of bromine to arylpropylenes of the general formulas R·CH₂·CH:CH₂ and R·CH:CH·CH₃, in which R denotes an etherified aryl radical; the addition of hydrobromic acid to these double bonds, however, had never previously been carried out. It has now been observed, unexpectedly, that hydrohalic acids, under suitable conditions, add to the unsaturated compounds named above to form the hitherto-unknown alkyloxy-, dialkyloxy-, or alkylenedioxyaryl halopropanes, without the cleavage of the alkyloxy group that might have been feared from the outset.

The addition of the hydrogen halide proceeds in such a way that the halogen attaches to the carbon atom nearer the benzene ring. The derivatives of allylbenzene — for example methyleugenol, safrole, apiol — accordingly yield isopropyl halides substituted (arylated) in the β-position: (Ar)·CH₂·CH:CH₂ + HBr = (Ar)·CH₂·CH(Br)·CH₃.

The derivatives of propenylbenzene — for example anethole, isosafrole — add hydrogen halide to form α-substituted (arylated) n-propyl halides: CH₃O·C₆H₄·CH:CH·CH₃ + HBr = CH₃O·C₆H₄·CH(Br)·CH₂·CH₃.

The resulting hydrogen-halide addition products are heavy, faintly coloured oils. They are comparatively unstable and cannot be distilled without decomposition, even in vacuo. Nevertheless, contrary to expectation, they react smoothly with ammonia and with primary aliphatic amines, giving the corresponding alkyloxy-, dialkyloxy-, or alkylenedioxyarylaminopropanes, or their N-monoalkyl derivatives.

This reaction was the less to be expected in that there was a risk that elimination of hydrohalic acid would simply regenerate the starting materials bearing the unsaturated side chain. In fact the reaction does proceed partly in this latter direction; this is, however, immaterial to the final result, since the recovered starting materials can always be returned to the reaction. The alkyloxy-, dialkyloxy-, and alkylenedioxyarylaminopropanes obtainable by reaction with ammonia or with monoalkylated ammonias are important intermediates for the preparation of therapeutically active compounds.

### Examples.

1. Hydrobromic acid is added to molten anethole in the manner set out in detail in Example 3, and the crude bromo compound so obtained is reacted, as there described, with alcoholic ammonia.

The resulting α-p-methoxyphenyl-n-propylamine is a colourless oil, boiling at 116–117° under a pressure of 7 mm. The hydrochloride salt melts at 217°.

2. The β-3,4-dimethoxyphenylisopropylamine obtained from methyleugenol in the same way is a colourless oil, boiling point 141–142° under 5 mm pressure. _[This pressure figure is uncertain in the scanned original — see textQuality notes.]_ The hydrochloride salt melts at 150–151°.

3. 150 g of safrole are introduced slowly, with ice-cooling, into 500 cc of a solution of hydrobromic acid in water saturated at 0°, and the mixture is shaken for several hours at the same temperature. The reaction product is taken up in chloroform; this solution is shaken successively with dilute soda solution and water, and dried over calcium chloride. On evaporating off the chloroform under reduced pressure, monobromodihydrosafrole remains, together with some unreacted safrole.

The reaction product is heated with four to five times its volume of strong aqueous ammonia for several hours at 120°, and the resulting base is isolated in the usual manner. _[This base is 3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine, MDA.]_

The compound is a colourless liquid boiling at 153° under 19 mm pressure; it forms an acid sulfate that crystallizes readily and well. The hydrochloride salt forms white needles melting at 183–185°.

4. 50 g of the crude bromodihydrosafrole obtained by the method described in Example 3 are heated with five times its volume of a strong alcoholic solution of methylamine for two hours at 130°. After removing the bulk of the methylamine, the residue is worked up in the usual manner. The new secondary base of the formula CH₂O₂:C₆H₃·CH₂·CH(CH₃):NH·CH₃ forms a colourless oil boiling at 155° under 20 mm pressure. _[This is N-methyl-3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine — MDMA.]_

The hydrochloride salt forms solid white crystals melting at 148–150°.

5. 50 g of isosafrole are introduced slowly, with ice-cooling, into 100 cc of a solution of hydrobromic acid in glacial acetic acid saturated at 0°, and the mixture is shaken for several hours. Work-up proceeds as described in Example 3.

The crude bromo compound so obtained is heated with four to five times its volume of saturated alcoholic ammonia for two hours at 100°. Ammonia and alcohol are removed in vacuo, and the base is isolated from the residue by the addition of excess alkali.

The α-3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl-n-propylamine boils at 141° under a pressure of 12 mm. The hydrochloride salt melts at 200–201°.

### Patent Claim:

A process for the preparation of alkyloxyaryl-, dialkyloxyaryl-, and alkylenedioxyarylaminopropanes, or their N-monoalkylated derivatives, consisting in treating the corresponding unsaturated propylene compounds of the general formulas R·CH₂·CH:CH₂ and R·CH:CH·CH₃ (R = alkoxyaryl, dialkoxyaryl, or alkylenedioxyaryl) with hydrohalic acids, and reacting the resulting halogen-containing reaction products with ammonia or primary aliphatic amines.

Berlin. Printed at the Reichsdruckerei.

_[Section heading: Teonanácatl, the Flesh of God]_

They had another kind of drunkenness that made them more cruel: this was with certain small mushrooms, which grow in this land as they do in Castile; but those of this land are of such a kind that, eaten raw, and being bitter, they drink after them, or eat with them, a little honey; and after a short while they would see a thousand visions, especially serpents, and as they went entirely out of their senses, it seemed to them that their legs and bodies were full of worms eating them alive, and so, half raving, they would go out of the house, wishing that someone would kill them; and from this bestial drunkenness and the affliction they felt, it sometimes happened that they hanged themselves, and they were also crueler toward others. These mushrooms they call in their language Teonanácatl, which means flesh of God — of the demon they worshipped; and in this manner, with that bitter food, their cruel god administered communion to them.

_[Section heading: Other Forms of Communion: The Rolls of Tezcatlipoca and Human Flesh]_

At many of their feasts they had the custom of making dough rolls, of many kinds, which they used almost as a communion of the god whose feast they were keeping; but they had one that more properly resembled communion, which was that in November, when they had gathered their maize and other seeds, from the seed of a kind of plant they called _[uncertain: "Xenixos"]_, with maize dough they made certain tamales — round rolls — which they cooked in water in a pot; and while these were cooking, some boys played a kind of drum, carved entirely from a single piece of wood, without hide or parchment; and they also sang and said that those rolls turned into the flesh of Tezcatlipoca, who was the god or demon they held greatest, to whom they attributed the most dignity; and only those boys ate those rolls in place of communion, or the flesh of that demon. The other Indians sought to eat the human flesh of those who died in sacrifice, and this was commonly eaten by the principal lords, and merchants, and the ministers of the temples; the common people rarely got so much as a mouthful of it. After the Spaniards had gone to war, and Mexico was already won, until the land was pacified, the Indians friendly to the Spaniards often ate of those they killed, because the Spaniards could not always forbid it; rather, at times, out of their need for the Indians, they let it pass, although they abhorred it.

translation_text:
### Contribution to the study of the toxic drinks of the Indians of the Northwest Amazon: ayahuasca — yajé — huánto

A comparative toxico-physiological study of a personal experience, by Dr. P. Reinburg, on mission for the Ministry of Public Instruction.

#### Ayahuasca and yajé

**Part 1. Introduction**

Aya-huasca (Quichua: liana of death, or of dreams, or of spirits), also called among the Indians of the Napo jayahuasca or yayahuasca (bitter liana), is a plant used by the Indians of certain tribes living in the territories watered by the left-bank tributaries of the upper Amazon (eastern Ecuador, Colombia, and southern Venezuela) to induce an intoxication — sometimes agitated, sometimes comatose — during which they have dreams and visions in which they foresee the future, discover their enemy, and so on.

During my stay in Iquitos (late 1912), several of my countrymen, employed in the large trading houses that carry on the rubber business in that small town, had spoken to me of ayahuasca, and claimed that after drinking it they had felt no unpleasant effect, only dreams of one kind or another.

It therefore seemed worthwhile to try this drink personally, and thereby contribute to the study of the toxic drinks of the Indians of the Amazon region.

For that reason, finding myself at San Antonio del Curaray (April–May 1913), staying with my friend the Ecuadorian Antonio Garcés, in the heart of Záparo country, and having learned that these Indians make use of ayahuasca, which they call *iyona*, I resolved to try its effects on myself.

I asked several Indians to prepare this drink for me. But from my very first words I could see that my request did not please them: their faces changed expression, their eyes evaded mine, and although they never refused outright, it was clear my request had little chance of being granted.

I had better luck, however, in approaching a non-Záparo Indian working for Garcés — a man named Teofilo, of Peruvian origin, I was told, though no more was specified. Having lived a long time at San Antonio and married to a Záparo woman, he had taken up the habit of drinking ayahuasca, and fairly often. I had cured him of a leg ulcer, and he was very grateful to me for it. I should add that he was of a much higher intellectual level than the other servants of the post. So when I asked him to prepare the ayahuasca for me, he raised only minor objections, agreed, and set about the necessary preparations.

The account that follows was written immediately after my experience, while I was still under the very strong impression it had left on me. I ask my readers' indulgence for the somewhat technical and precise detail it contains.

**Personal experience**

*May 1.* — In an earthenware pot (Quichua: *manga*) in which nothing had ever been cooked with salt, Teofilo put a liter and a half of water, four pieces of ayahuasca thirty centimeters long, pounded and chopped, and five or six leaves of yajé.

From 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. he boiled the whole down to a quarter of a liter, over a fire of *pona* wood — said to be the best, because it "cooks harder" (*cocina mas duro*).

We had arranged to meet that evening at 9 p.m., that is, after everyone at the post had gone to bed, to drink the preparation. It was essential, Teofilo had explained to me, to be in darkness and silence, so that the action would take effect, so that the dreams would develop, and so that "one could see the future clearly."

At the appointed hour, when all was silent, Teofilo arrived carrying a *maté* (gourd) full of the brew, accompanied by his ten-year-old son César, who had already taken ayahuasca several times.

I stretched out in a chambira-fiber hammock hung in the outer corridor of the house, took the maté, which was filled with a cloudy brown liquid, unpleasant to look at, and, putting out the lamp, swallowed at one draught the amount of a teacupful — the average dose for a man. If it was unpleasant to look at, what of the taste! It is acrid, bitter, nauseating, leaving in the mouth a truly disagreeable aftertaste.

There was nothing left for me to do but wait for events to unfold. Young César had drunk after me; as for his father, who wanted to join us, I had asked him to abstain so that he could watch over us.

We remained thus for an hour, in absolute silence; still the dreams did not come.

The pulse, however, was slowed, though strongly marked; a kind of numbness came over me, a tendency toward sleep against which I struggled on account of the vampire bats that were circling above me and would not have failed to take advantage of the slightest moment of sleep. My jaw muscles are tetanized, I have a touch of trismus; when I try to open my jaws my teeth chatter against each other, and when I bring them together a contraction clenches them tight. There is some difficulty in swallowing saliva, and I have almost a sensation of paralysis of the muscles of the neck and larynx. Before my eyes shine several luminous circles, phosphenes, and I see, flying in a dazzling sky, a few butterflies belonging to the species collected that morning, which are abundant here. My sight is very sharp, too sharp, and it seems to me that I am seeing through a small hole pierced in a card; my intelligence seems overexcited, my power of observation highly developed; I record all the symptoms with perfect lucidity of mind and witness all the events as though they concerned someone else — a symptom that struck me in particular. I have pains in my ears; salivation is excessive; I have no nausea. Now, Teofilo had explained to me, nausea (*mareación*) is the forewarning sign of the dreams.

Meanwhile young César was thrashing on the ground, moaning, in the grip of violent nausea without vomiting, to the great satisfaction of his father, who declared that his son was about to set off for the land of dreams. This was not long in coming, and soon, growing calm, he fell into a deep sleep.

Toward 11 p.m., seeing that nothing was happening, and that I was not enjoying the same bliss as César, I mentioned it to Teofilo, who then gave me a second maté, of which I swallowed two or three good mouthfuls. A quarter of an hour later I felt all the previous symptoms intensify, and nausea set in. My mind is highly overexcited; it seems to me that my body has disappeared; I am nothing but a brain observing, with interest, the phases of an experiment happening to someone else.

The pulse is very slow, but I do not know how many beats per minute; blood pressure is greatly reduced, at least as far as I can tell by touch; then the pulse becomes imperceptible at moments, and the nausea increases. Not feeling well, I mention it to Teofilo, who reassures me by saying that this is all as it should be, that the beneficial action (!) of the ayahuasca is beginning, and that I am going to have dreams.

Not very reassured all the same, I have my lamp lit and ask for a mirror: I am ghastly pale, my dilated pupils do not react to light, my hands make clonic, jerky, rapid movements whenever I try to grasp something. The earache has worsened, but my hearing is perfect; the nausea increases and becomes very unpleasant; and, abandoning the precepts of ayahuasca drinkers, who hold that one should let the symptoms subside on their own, I want with all my strength to vomit and to drink tea, especially because my heart worries me. I get up (midnight), urinate copiously, having difficulty standing, and take the two or three steps that separate me from my room, where I want to light the stove to make tea. But there I am seized with weakness and fall like a dead weight onto a trunk, crying out to Teofilo, "I am poisoned." My pulse has vanished completely, I am ghastly pale, my pupils dilated, my throat tight with severe difficulty swallowing, my mouth dry, a sensation that the lower half of my body has disappeared, my hands moving in disorder as I try to grasp something; trismus very pronounced, speech very difficult and halting. I can only give brief orders to poor Teofilo, who is distressed and assures me that it is not poison, that I should have stayed lying down, and so on. He prepares tea, opens my medicine kit, from which I have him bring out tannin, granulated Houdé caffeine, and an ampoule of caffeine, with which I want to give myself a subcutaneous injection; but although everything is there, within reach of my hand, I cannot make a single movement, and I feel that if someone wanted to kill me, I would be unable to defend myself, so utterly am I annihilated.

I have myself laid out flat on a sharply reclined deck chair and drink at least a liter of very strong tea. I cannot vomit; I then put a finger down my throat: the reflex has vanished, and I can put my finger behind the roof of my palate without provoking it. I then take 0.50 to 0.60 centigrams of tannin, then, some time later, ipecac, and at last very copious vomiting comes, three times, after unbelievable effort. I have an intense headache and feel quite cold, although it is +25°. I go on drinking tea and vomit a second time, very copiously. My pulse begins to be perceptible again — thready, intermittent, very faint. I have very strong coffee prepared, which I take with five or six teaspoons of Houdé granulated caffeine, and drink at least a liter of it. Sleep is irresistible; my breathing resembles Cheyne-Stokes respiration; each time sleep overcomes me, my breathing stops, and so does my pulse. I then inhale ether, which brings on great, deep breaths.

While this succession of events unfolds, my mind never once ceases observing and recording; I am perfectly aware of my condition, know what needs to be done, but cannot do it; fortunately I have Teofilo's help — alone, I could do nothing.

*May 2.* — Toward 2 a.m., the vomiting having stopped, and my pulse becoming better marked though still dicrotic, I am helped to bed and lie down fully dressed. Little by little my pulse increases in rate and strength, my circulation feels better; on the other hand, the headache (especially a frontal headache, a kind of vise gripping my skull) is very intense. The trismus persists. Tingling begins to run through my whole body, my extremities, which had been icy, grow warm again, and I sweat a little.

Toward 3 a.m., in less than half an hour, I urinate four times, very copiously (at least two and a half to three liters). My sight remains just as sharp, my speech less halting, my general state improves. I still need to inhale ether from time to time, whenever my breathing threatens to stop. I then take one last cup of strong coffee, and toward four o'clock, my pulse being if not normal then nearly regular, very rapid, and strongly marked, I let myself give way to the sleep against which I had struggled until then, and do not wake again until about 9 a.m.

I get up dazed, battered, broken, and drag myself out of the room. I have no strength to speak; I have a splitting headache and no appetite, with the difficulty swallowing still present. I take magnesium sulfate and a little tea and spend my day in the hammock. In the afternoon, my pulse still tending to grow thin, I take a little more granulated caffeine. In the evening I go to bed early and sleep soundly.

As for young César, he had a very bad headache all day, but did not complain of it, delighted at having had beautiful dreams. Old Teofilo came to see me several times. He seemed rather crestfallen, for he had not expected to see such a result in me.

*May 3.* — I feel much better: pulse normal, but still a little frontal headache. I swallow well and eat with a good appetite.

But it is only on May 4 that I can say I feel in my normal state, and even then, over the next two or three days, I still have some difficulty swallowing from time to time.

**Plants used to prepare the drink**

At my request, Teofilo took me into the forest to see the plant he had used to make his brew: it is a liana, *huasca* (whence *ayahuasca*), about the thickness of a thumb. I took a few pieces of it, but they were later unfortunately lost, along with other collections that my abrupt departure for France in August 1914 forced me to leave behind in Ecuador. Generally, Indians who have found an ayahuasca vine always carefully hide it from their friends, so as to keep its enjoyment for themselves.

As for the yajé, which also enters into the composition of the brew, it was shown to me at San Antonio, beside an Indian house where it was cultivated: it is a small shrub, 4.5 meters tall, with petiolate leaves (petiole 15 mm long), entire, oval, 20 cm long, 7 cm wide, regular and ending in a point 2 cm long. I did not observe any flowers. This shrub is frequently found near houses, where the Indians tend it with care, whereas ayahuasca is most often found in the forest.

**Uses of ayahuasca among the Záparo**

The Záparo, as we have said, use this drink, prepared from ayahuasca alone or mixed with yajé, to induce dreams from which they draw conclusions about the future. Living in the forest, their minds occupied with the struggle for existence, it is not surprising that their principal visions are of the tiger, the serpent, the enemies of neighboring tribes (the Jívaro in particular, and the Tukano), or else the animals they encounter and hunt in the course of their forest expeditions: various birds, monkeys, tapirs, deer, and so on.

Before venturing on any expedition (war, forest hunting, the search for rubber, etc.), the Záparo never fail to drink ayahuasca.

Apart from this special circumstance of foreseeing the future, it seems they also have the custom of drinking ayahuasca purely for pleasure, somewhat like the opium addict who, having first sought a new sensation in opium, ends up smoking it from habit and need. Thus at San Antonio certain Indians took ayahuasca once a week, seeking, they claimed, no other pleasure than that of getting drunk cheaply, *cachaça* (cane brandy) being scarce and expensive. But most of them saw it above all as a practice of sorcery, and used it as such.

Some drink two to three times the dose that I absorbed.

The sorcerers — *brujos* in Spanish, *tapia* in Quichua — make frequent use of this drink mixed with yajé, especially those who practice medical sorcery. When a Záparo sorcerer goes to see a sick person, which always takes place at night, he never fails to take the drink prepared as I have described above, but in successive rather than massive doses (his mithridatism, moreover, allows him to withstand the toxin better than I was able to). Thus, in his sleep, he comes to learn the illness that the spirits reveal to him, and on waking, by applying his mouth to the painful area and sucking, he draws out the *chunta* (a small thorn or splinter of the palm *Bactris ciliata* Mart., or a piece of wood, or even a seed, etc.) which he has first taken care to place in his own mouth — the said chunta being always held to be the cause of the illness, and to have come from some enemy who "sent" it into the sick person's body. The sorcerer then indicates where it came from and who sent it, and the patient prepares to take revenge on whoever cast this evil spell on him.

Although it is not, strictly speaking, an ordeal-drink, the act of drinking ayahuasca nevertheless confers, as I was able to observe for myself, a certain standing in the eyes of the Indians. Záparo sorcerers are in fact renowned and feared among the Indians of Canelos.

It is certain that once these Indians learned I had taken ayahuasca and yajé, they placed in my medical care a trust mixed with still greater respect and fear. "For," they said, "if I could cure them, then I could obviously also make them sick." I took care not to disabuse them, for fear of losing all standing.

_[The article continues with a second part, "Comparison with similar drinks described by other travelers" — a critical review of the observations of Spruce, Crevaux, Villavicencio, and others — followed by botanical, etymological, and chemical sections (pp. 33–54), omitted here in order to focus on the author's personal experience and his direct ethnographic observations.]_

translation_text:
### Documents toward a study of yagé

VARIETIES

In 1903, a Colombian naturalist, [Dr.] Rafael Zerda Bayón, returning from a scientific expedition through the little-known territories of the Colombian Caquetá and the Putumayo, brought back — along with a rich harvest of documents and raw materials of vegetable origin — a liana wreathed in a strange and marvelous legend: yagé. By makeshift means he isolated from it a crude alkaloid, to which, for reasons that will become clear, he gave the unexpected name of telepathine.

The interest awakened by this "plant of the prophets" prompted other Colombian researchers to take up its study. G. Fischer Cárdenas, in 1923, made it the subject of a short medical thesis. Mrs. Georgina Muñoz v. de Salinas undertook, around the same time, a series of interesting psycho-physiological trials soon to be published.

Quite recently, Professor Barriga Villalba of the University of Bogotá, having abundant material at his disposal, took up and carried further the chemical study of yagé.

He was the first to isolate, in crystallized form, and to study Zerda Bayón's alkaloid, renaming it, more appropriately, yagéine. He further discovered a second alkaloid, which he called yagénine.

What follows is a translation of his work, published in the *Boletín de la Sociedad Colombiana de Ciencias Naturales* of Bogotá, March 1923.

A. Rouhier.

### I. A New Alkaloid: Yagéine

"In the vast Colombian regions of the Putumayo and Caquetá rivers grows a plant that the inhabitants of these regions call yagé.

"The Indians prepare from this plant a special drink, by decoction of the woody stem cut into pieces roughly a span long. They concentrate the liquor by boiling it down to a tenth of its volume, add water, and concentrate it again. The result is a reddish liquid with greenish tones which, after settling, turns topaz-colored and shows a beautiful blue-green fluorescence.

"The natives drink quantities of about 60 cm³ of this liquor, each dose equivalent to roughly 0.50 g of alkaloids. They drink it either at great, solemn ceremonies or in private. For this they use a special vessel they call a *mate*.

"The Indian under the influence of yagé ends up intoxicated (which also happens to whites), and yet, according to trustworthy people who have lived among them, no poisonings appear to have been recorded. Under the plant's effect, the Indians leap, shout, run in every direction, and let out cries in imitation of forest animals. When the effects wear off, they intoxicate themselves again by drinking more of the liquor, and this can go on for days at a time.

"The effects of the drink have been greatly exaggerated by white people who claim to have taken it. They say it brings on divination, the vision of the future, distant (telepathic) and extraretinal vision, and many other effects that are far from the truth. We can affirm the contrary, on the basis of the experiments we have carried out with the pure salts of the alkaloid.

"The plant has the appearance of a sparsely leaved shrub that tends to twine around neighboring trunks. Its maximum height does not exceed 3 to 4 m. The maximum diameter of the trunk is 5 dm. The leaves are opposite and olive-green in color.

"It grows at a minimum altitude of 700 m, in a climate where the temperature exceeds 28° centigrade.

"It contains two alkaloids that crystallize readily. The more important is present in a proportion of 1.50% of the dry plant, the other at 0.023%. It also contains an acid whose lime salt crystallizes well; this is probably what saturates the alkaloids. The plant also contains a dichroic coloring matter that oxidizes readily in air, turning scarlet red. A small amount of fatty matter and a resin are also found.

"We have designated the principal alkaloid yagéine, and the other, yagénine.

_[A detailed account follows in the original of the chemical extraction method, the physical and crystallographic properties of yagéine, a solubility table, the elemental analysis and proposed formula (C₁₂H₈N₂O), the color reactions with various alkaloid reagents, and a table of lethal doses in the guinea pig (from 0.10 g, fatal in 9 hours, to 1 gram, fatal in 10 minutes). This purely chemical and animal-toxicological material is omitted here.]_

"In summary, yagéine is an alkaloid that produces general anesthesia, and whose applications hold a certain promise as a medicine particularly selective for certain organs; it neither touches nor alters the other essential functions."

A. M. Barriga Villalba, M.A., D.Ph.,
Professor of Chemistry at the University of Bogotá.
(Translated by A. Rouhier.)

### II. Supplementary Notes on Yagé

Yagé is a liana native to the great tropical forests of the upper Amazon basin.

Its range therefore extends across several South American countries: upper Brazil, Venezuela, Peru, Colombia, and perhaps Guiana. It also spills over onto the Pacific slope of the Cordillera, where the liana is known by the name *pildé*.

Yagé is thought to be an Apocynaceae: *Haemadictyon amazonicum* Benth. The recent death of the Colombian botanist Santiago Cortés made it impossible to confirm this identification. The various samples that have recently reached France — thanks to the active kindness of Mr. Pinto Valderrama, of His Excellency Count Dejean, and to the courtesy of Mrs. G. Muñoz and Mr. L. Marulanda of Cali — unfortunately lacked flowers and fruit, and so did not permit it either.

Some of the material we have been able to examine so far even leads us to suspect that plants of different varieties or species may be grouped under the same name of yagé (the yagé of the Putumayo, the yagé of Naya, for example).

Dr. Reinburg published a study on yagé in France in 1921, as did Professor Em. Perrot in 1923, and we ourselves in 1924.

What is the action of yagé? It obviously varies according to dose, and also according to the race of the experimenter.

We have been able to establish that small doses (50 to 100 drops of the 1:5 tincture) produce mild nervous stimulation, expressed as a feeling of well-being, mental activity, and muscular alacrity, similar to that of caffeine-like substances and, in truth, to that of many stimulants of the intellect. Slight pupil dilation is observed.

With stronger doses (5 to 10 cc of the 1:5 tincture) a marked tendency toward sleep follows the more pronounced initial phase of excitement. This sleep is characterized by great activity of dream production.

Still higher doses — from the 30 g of stems used in the native manner, as a decoction, in Mrs. G. Muñoz's experiments, which must correspond approximately to 0.50 or 0.60 g of alkaloids, up to the much higher amounts to which only the Indian devotees of yagé are accustomed — produce the following effects:

First, broad blue glimmers seem to haloe external objects, or even color them entirely with an intense azure glow.

Then hallucinations occur, sometimes of incomparable beauty and great vividness of color, recalling in this respect the visions of peyote or hashish, and sometimes frightening and horrible.

As with peyote as well, and as a result of the excitation of the cerebral center of vision, visual sensitivity is heightened, to the point that the person under yagé is able to perceive objects in near-total darkness. Another phenomenon, probably of the same origin, occurs that we will not describe in more explicit terms, since we have not observed it personally: the subject feels as though his eyes "are made of crystal": "Everything I see," says one of them, "is as if 'caught' by the pupil" (*todo lo veo como prendido de la pupila*). Another tells the person beside him that he can see the inside of his own body (*que estaba viéndome interiormente mis entrañas*). The Caverres Indians use almost identical terms in attributing a similar power to yagé.

Here, then, produced by the drug, is a whole series of visual anomalies that it will be interesting to study more closely.

Then the patient abruptly gives way to an overpowering, deep sleep, during which his insensibility becomes almost total.

The acceleration of the subconscious imagination produced by the drug fills this sleep with dreams of astonishing precision and clarity, some of which, apparently taking on a metagnomic [paranormal-knowledge] character, have helped to give yagé, in popular belief, its solid reputation as a magical, divinatory herb.

On waking, the person under yagé describes all the visions he has undergone, which remain strongly etched in his memory: visions of coming events, of distant scenes, of stolen or lost objects, of fantastic figures, of marvelous landscapes, of journeys made through cities or across unknown lands.

These images of the yagé dream have a clear tendency to be now micropsic, now megalopsic. In the sleeping state they reproduce the lilliputian hallucinations observed and described by Dr. Leroy, and those other, gigantic ones which, by antilogy, we shall call "brobdingnagian" — both of which are found in many toxic deliriums, in cocaine psychoses, and so on, and which are also produced by ayahuasca and by peyote.

It is curious to note that missionaries — hardly to be suspected of bias in the matter — do not deny the metagnomic phenomena brought on by yagé, as appears from one of their letters: "As for the divination of the future, an infinity of facts are cited for which, at first sight, it is not easy to find an explanation... Perfectly honest people, even some of some virtue, have taken yagé out of curiosity, intending to recover lost objects. They themselves were astonished at the surprising result they obtained. It would seem, then, that this is a plant of very active properties, which excites the nervous system and plunges one into a kind of hypnosis — something that certain people put to bad use."

Very high doses of yagé are used on the occasion of ritual ceremonies and in practices of religious magic by numerous Indian tribes, several of them cannibalistic. They use the stems and sometimes the leaves, in very concentrated decoctions, which they sometimes reinforce further with other plants of more formidable physiological activity: aya-huesca (*Banisteria Caapi* Spr.), tobacco, huanto (*Datura arborea*). Such drinks — some so dangerous that they are used only by sorcerers and medicine men — confer on those who take them a kind of initiation, and the intoxication they produce, as dangerous as that obtained from the potions consumed in certain African ordeals, is held to be a true communion with the gods.

The doses of yagé are then so massive that the Indian, seized by a furious delirium, believes himself changed into a beast — tiger, cobra, tapir, etc. — and runs here and there, imitating the animal's cries and gait. Sometimes, having reached an intense degree of nervous excitement, he tries to throw himself upon those he meets, to devour them.

_[Remarks follow on the anthelmintic action of yagé observed by Mrs. Muñoz, and technical detail on the assay of the official 1:5 tincture; this purely analytical passage is omitted.]_

We had occasion to examine a liquid Indian preparation of yagé, made by a tribe of Jívaro near Macas, Peru.

Characteristics: an aqueous vegetable decoction, very cloudy, yellowish in color, with a slightly acid litmus reaction. Density at 15° = 1.030. Already beginning to spoil. Faint taste, very slightly bitter and astringent, not at all unpleasant. A faintly alcoholic smell, although the liquor contains no alcohol.

Seen at a certain angle, it shows a very slight fluorescence, which becomes more pronounced on dilution with a little alcohol.

Acids slightly pale its color but do not clarify the liquid. Alkalis turn it blood-red, and then, with time and exposure to air, red-brown.

It contains a brown sediment, part of which has settled on the walls and bottom of the bottle. This sediment (unweighed), formed in part of woody and earthy matter, contains an alkaloidal substance characterized as yagéine.

Filtered and evaporated, it leaves 5.40% dry residue.

Assayed by the same procedure as the tincture, this decoction shows an alkaloid content of 0.26%. This alkaloid is yagéine, showing all of its reactions.

A. Rouhier.

_[Author's note:]_ This preparation was sent by our Minister of France in Quito to His Excellency Count Dejean, who kindly forwarded it to us.

summary: S. Weir Mitchell's account of his own peyote self-experiment on May 24, 1896, read before the American Neurological Society. Mitchell describes detailed visions and includes a second self-experiment by a colleague, Dr. Eshner, with physiological notes and subjective observations.
abstract: S. Weir Mitchell's account of his own peyote self-experiment on May 24, 1896, read before the American Neurological Society. Mitchell describes detailed visions and includes a second self-experiment by a colleague, Dr. Eshner, with physiological notes and subjective observations.
editorial_note: Text pass: hand-checked. Transcription confidence: medium. The previous transcript filled two badly disordered stretches of the scan (BMJ pp. 1627-1628, covering the end of the vision sequence and Mitchell's ensuing discussion of migraine auras) by reordering surviving OCR word-fragments into grammatical sequence. That is not transcription and has been removed. In its place: the genuinely scrambled clause about his attentiveness during the visions ('...notes for future use') is cut and marked illegible; a badly duplicated/mirrored OCR fragment following the opal passage is dropped outright; a boxed quotation of a migraine patient's visual aura that interrupts the page twice is marked as omitted rather than silently skipped; and the whole 'megrim' discussion section, which is genuinely out of reading order in the scan, is now covered by an honest editorial bracket instead of being invented. Two short sentence fragments broken only by an ordinary page turn ('I sought so to limit...full possession of all my faculties' and the joined opal sentence) were rejoined, which is standard OCR repair, not reconstruction. Separately, this pass also restored a large amount of text -- roughly 750 words across both Mitchell's account and Dr. Eshner's -- that was clean and fully legible in the raw scan but had been silently dropped or ellipsised ('...') in the prior transcript without any editorial mark: the morphine-vision aside, Eshner's pulse readings, his bicycle-ride detail, and similar passages. 'Red and green' (previously left as '[illegible]') is restored on strong internal evidence -- the very next sentence independently reads 'the tints of intense green and red shifted and altered' -- and 'vivid green' has been corrected to 'level green', which is what the raw scan actually shows. Two small remaining gaps near the end of Eshner's account are marked illegible in place rather than guessed. This was not a full sentence-by-sentence audit of every line in Eshner's appendix; a human editor should still skim pp. 1628-1629 against the raw file for anything missed.
citation: S. Weir Mitchell, "Remarks on the Effects of Anhelonium Lewinii (the Mescal Button)," British Medical Journal 2, no. 1875 (December 5, 1896): 1625–1629.
